Soirée dialogue, construction identitair: Dialogue Night, Identity Formation: Neither From Here Nor From Elsewhere?

La thématique de cette soirée dialogue m: The theme of this dialogue night touches me personally. It’s a subject I had wanted to dig into for a while. As a child of immigrants myself, the questions raised during this conversation are part of my everyday life.
J’ai donc voulu créer un espace de discu: So I wanted to create an authentic, safe space for discussion where young Montréal adults could share their views. Some were there to represent community organizations rooted in different neighbourhoods across the city, but above all to share their lived experiences.
<strong>Jeudi 12 juin dernier, six Montr: Last Thursday, June 12, six Montrealers gathered at the offices of La Converse. Maria, Ikram, Karim, Charline, Luce and Sydney all share a story tied to immigration. They were born in their countries of origin and immigrated to Quebec at a very young age, or they were born in the Greater Montréal area and come from multiple cultures. We spent nearly two hours talking about how they have built their identities.
Ils prennent place dans le salon où les: They take their seats in the living room, where the chairs are arranged in an arc. While waiting for all the guests to arrive, the conversation stays light. Everyone gradually gets to know each other without revealing too much about why they are here; they save those answers for the recording.
Vers 18h30, tout le monde est prêt. Les: Around 6:30 p.m., everyone is ready. The official introductions begin. Maria, in her thirties, works for the youth program of the Centre d'aide aux familles latino-américaines (<l1>CAFLA</l1>). Questions around identity formation affect her deeply, both in her work, with the people she serves every day, and in her personal development.
Ikram a le même âge que Maria, elles son: Ikram is the same age as Maria, and the two have been friends since childhood. Ikram has worked extensively in the community sector, with various immigrant populations considered vulnerable. That is why she wanted to be here.
Luce n’a pas précisé son âge, ni son mét: Luce did not share her age or her profession. She was invited by Ikram and Maria and joined in, listening closely to the discussion.
Charline est à Montréal depuis cinq mois: Charline has been in Montréal for only five months. She is not Québécoise. She was born in Hawaii, in the United States, and her parents are from Hong Kong. She is slowly adjusting to her new surroundings and likes to step outside her comfort zone. She is more comfortable in English, but makes a remarkable effort to share her experience in French.
Sydney travaille auprès de jeunes du sec: Sydney works with high school students. For her, this discussion is a chance to put forward answers, strategies and solutions to the identity crises that most of the young people she works with go through. She also represents the organization <l1>Brique par Brique</l1>, which fights for access to social housing in the Parc Extension neighbourhood.
Karim représente l’organisme <l1>Philo-B: Karim represents the organization <l1>Philo-Boxe</l1>, based in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood. He and his team combine boxing lessons with philosophical discussions for local youth. He is also in his thirties.
<strong>Comment définit-on son identité: How do you define your identity when you come from a plurality of cultures?
Cette première question, au centre de ce: This first question, at the heart of the evening, opens the discussion for our participants. Slowly, hands go up. Everyone has something to say, opinions to share.
Ikram prend le micro la première. Elle p: Ikram is the first to take the microphone. She pushes her glasses up onto her head and adjusts her Palestinian keffiyeh over her shoulders. All eyes are on her, very attentive. She was born in Algeria and fled terrorism and the civil war with her parents in the 1990s. So she did not come from economic immigration, she clarifies. For her, it was the violence of their journey that pushed her parents to distance her as much as possible from her roots.
« Mes parents m’ont dit : “Tu vas être Q: “My parents told me: ‘You’re going to be Québécoise. As Québécoise as you can be. You’re going to speak French!’ So I don’t speak Arabic, but I understand it,” she points out. As a child, she therefore did everything she could to fit in and look like her Québécois classmates, erasing her Algerian roots. Over the years, her parents were able to calm their anger toward their country of origin and returned to their culture and their religion.
Ikram retourne souvent auprès de sa fami: Ikram often goes back to visit her family, but once there, she is treated differently too. “Even though I was welcomed, I was never able to fully fit in over there, even on vacation,” she says in a serious tone. In short, for Ikram, building her identity is a long and painful process that is still ongoing.
Le micro est ensuite tendu à Maria. Elle: The microphone is then handed to Maria. She too adjusts the keffiyeh on her shoulders. Maria wears glasses with yellow-tinted lenses, and her dark hair is pulled back into a sleek bun. She begins her story: “I’m of Colombian origin. I was born there, both my parents are from Cali. I arrived when I was 5. I immigrated with my mother, who raised me on her own here. At the time, I think we were fleeing some of the violence that followed the Pablo Escobar era and narcoterrorism.”
Maria a passé son enfance dans des école: Maria spent her childhood in mostly white schools. Like Ikram, she fit in as much as possible, notably by adopting the Québécois accent, she explains. For her, a large part of identity formation happens through language. She felt a lot of opposition between her two cultures. The title of the evening – Neither From Here Nor From Elsewhere – therefore resonates strongly with her: “You’re never Québécoise enough, but you’re never Latina enough to be who you are. You’re always, constantly in duality with these identities.”
Avec le temps, Maria a réussi à trouver: Over time, Maria has managed to find a balance that works for her. For her, working in her mother tongue is important. “I maintain that link with my community. I keep that sense of belonging,” she says happily.
Karim prend ensuite la parole. Il repren: Karim speaks next. He picks up the concept of duality raised by Maria. He was born and raised in Montréal, in the Côte-des-Neiges neighbourhood, and is originally from Guadeloupe. He also lives with not being considered Québécois in Quebec, nor Guadeloupean in his country of origin.
Aujourd’hui, les bases de son identité s: Today, the foundations of his identity are clear: “I define myself as Black. I define myself as part of the Creole identity. I define myself much more as a Montrealer than anything else.”
Son travail auprès des jeunes de son qua: His work with the youth of his neighbourhood and the many relationships built over his lifetime have shaped who he is: “I went through pretty much every school system possible: French, Québécois, private, public. I met many types of people, many types of identities. So I know just how fragile identity is.”
Karim se qualifie d’anarchiste, sur le t: Karim jokingly calls himself an anarchist. He’s not a fan of the systems in place, whatever they may be. “I grew up in a very, very multicultural neighbourhood, in Côte-des-Neiges. I never really felt a break [with Québécois culture], except in the school systems. I had friends who were Sri Lankan, Latino, Filipino. It was like a balance. None of them dominated the others. Whereas when you go into institutions, of course someone dominates the other. There’s a specific way of thinking, a way of acting, a way of doing things …”
Il a du mal à s’identifier à la culture: He has trouble identifying with Québécois culture. He has often felt pushed aside, that he was “the other.” He recognizes several similarities between Guadeloupean culture and Quebec’s, notably in language and in identity struggles, but it doesn’t move him much.
Charline, à l'autre extrémité du cercle,: Charline, at the other end of the circle, continues the discussion. She has her back to the cameras and faces the rest of the group. She speaks in a low voice, almost whispering. In Hawaii, she never felt different from those around her, since there is a very large Asian community on the island. She grew up alongside children of immigrants, mostly from East Asia.
C’est à son arrivée à Montréal que son r: It was when she arrived in Montréal that her relationship to cultural differences changed. “I really felt my ethnic difference, especially in Montréal. I felt that a lot, much more than when I went to study in the United States. I feel like it might be a language thing. French is quite difficult to learn. Coming here, I sought out time with communities of people from diverse backgrounds,” she confides.
Elle n’arrive pas encore à mettre le doi: She still can’t put her finger on what is different in the city compared to the other places she has lived: “Maybe it’s because of a cultural element I’m not aware of, that I haven’t fully absorbed. But I don’t know, I feel like it’s a bit hard to express exactly what’s going on here, what made me feel that way.”
Maria est la première à prendre la parol: Maria is the first to speak on this second question. She takes a moment to think and explains: “Our identity isn’t fixed. It evolves over time, through our perception of the world, our perception of ourselves, our culture, our baggage and our experiences.” The rest of the participants nod in agreement.
Plus concrètement, les aller-retour vers: More concretely, trips back and forth to her country of origin have allowed her to recharge and reconnect with her roots, which life in Quebec had left somewhat neglected. Maria is also grateful to have grown up in the heart of Montréal, alongside a variety of cultures. “It strengthens my identity. I’m very open-minded because of it, it opens me up to certain realities I might not have known in other contexts,” she points out.
Karim prend ensuite le micro. Pour lui,: Karim then takes the microphone. For him, the strongest elements of his identity formation come from his inner circle: his neighbourhood, his family, his friends. He then adds a nuance about what, in his view, makes all the difference in how we build ourselves. “I sincerely believe identity isn’t a problem as long as you’re not in a system. It’s not a problem being with the other as long as you’re not in a system that confronts you with the other, that confronts you either with your skin colour or your gender. Otherwise we can live together, in my opinion.” The systems, as Karim calls them, are spaces that can be tied to education, health, the workplace or many others.
Il a été confronté à des situations où i: He has faced situations where he had to more or less justify his presence in professional spaces, where he became aware of his difference in front of a majority that didn’t look like him. “I’m a manager and I sit on a community roundtable. So I walk into a system. And it’s once I’m in that system that I tell myself: ‘Ok, oh s**t , I'm black as f**k,’” he says, laughing.
<strong>« Ma construction identitaire n': “My identity formation isn’t finished because I’m angry, I’m furious. I’m full of resentment.”
<strong>- Ikram, participante de la Soir: – Ikram, participant in the Dialogue Night, Identity Formation: Neither From Here Nor From Elsewhere?
Ikram est la suivante à répondre. Les di: Ikram is next to respond. The stories shared have moved her. Anger makes her voice tremble. What frustrates her, notably, is her relationship with the Algerian diaspora in the city: “I’m 32, and I’ve never been so angry in my life. I’ve been in white spaces all my life. I’m not embarrassed to talk about it: my community rejected me here. I went to school with them, I was trying to fit in with them, I was trying to get into those circles, but my community wanted nothing to do with me.”
Elle ajoute : « Ma construction identita: She adds: “My identity formation isn’t finished because I’m angry, I’m furious. I’m full of resentment. I try [to calm myself] every day of my life, and that’s why I appreciate it so much when my friends introduce me to settings like this one. (...). To try, precisely, to attach myself to something that can just ease a little of this anger and this pain, because there’s nothing that can fix it.”
Sydney poursuit la conversation. Elle a: Sydney continues the conversation. She recently realized the significant impact of the people involved in her community. The organization Brique par Brique gives meaning to who she is. “I met so many people who have concerns similar to mine. And we talked about those concerns. And it was so healing to have that,” she says with a gentle smile.
<strong>Quel est votre rapport avec la q: What is your relationship with the question “Where are you from?”
Pour la première fois, Luce prend la par: For the first time, Luce speaks. This question seems to stir something in her. She has been very attentive and silent throughout the discussion, but she has a lot to say about the infamous “Where are you from?”
« Je ne réponds même plus, je me dis : “: “I don’t even answer anymore, I just think: ‘Come on!’ For me, when people ask that question, it’s already to create a divide. You’re ‘them’ and I’m ‘the other.’ It’s already creating an identity divide. It’s to establish that we’re different,” she explains calmly.
Luce a souvent eu l’impression d’être ob: Luce has often had the feeling of being watched. A heavy gaze that has profoundly shaped her identity formation. She feels judged by a majority that celebrates the individual successes of Black people but attributes their failures to the entire community. This double standard has placed on her, for far too long, a crushing sense of responsibility. “When you build your identity around that, you risk always building your identity in someone else’s gaze,” she adds.
Maria acquiesce et rebondit : « J’ai l’h: Maria nods and picks up the thread: “I’m used to being asked. I think it depends on how it’s asked and by whom. It affects how I’m going to receive it.” All the participants agree. For everyone, if the question comes from someone with an immigrant background, it’s necessarily out of sincere curiosity. Conversely, misplaced curiosity, fetishization and ignorance are poorly received.
<strong>Quels éléments représentent le p: Which elements represent your identity the most now? What represents home for you?
La réponse qui est revenue le plus souve: The answer that came up most often was to attach oneself to Montréal as the place where one feels good, a little more at peace, at home. It’s where family, friends and the people who shape one’s personality are.
Maria ressent une évolution dans son att: Maria feels a shift in her attachment to the city. The community sector where she has worked for several years now has shown her a darker, less inclusive side of the city where she grew up. She finds the social and political context harder on newcomers, and it exasperates her. Ikram agrees with her.
L’algérienne d’origine empoigne son keff: The Algerian-born woman grabs her keffiyeh and adds: “I feel at home through my struggles! With everything that’s happening in Palestine, everything that’s happening around immigration. I find a bit of myself every time I’m in a community fighting for something bigger than us. It gives me back a bit of my humanity.”
Pour Karim, ce qui le forgera toujours,: For Karim, what will always shape him is something spiritual, his emotional connection with the people in his life. “What represents my home is always my neighbourhood, but also always something deeper. It’s being with people, being surrounded by love, my family, my daughter,” he says.
Sydney rejoint cette pensée : « Ça va so: Sydney echoes this thought: “This is going to sound a bit cheesy, but for me, home is when I’m surrounded by people like you. Talking together, we vibe on another level, a spiritual level.” All the participants smile and nod.
La soirée touche à sa fin, les échanges: The evening is drawing to a close, and the conversation drifts somewhat. Almost all of the participants work with community organizations and with young people, so they share their experiences and points of view.
Au bout d’une heure et demie de discussi: After an hour and a half of discussion, the dialogue night ends with applause and thanks.

Maria tient à mettre de l’avant sa persp: Maria is keen to put forward her intersectional perspective. And me, I’m single, I’m pansexual. I only came out recently. All of these things expose me to certain things, to a complexity, on another level.”
